query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Forming a thicker and more stable oxide tribofilm at higher post-deposition annealing temperature is the primary factor that improves wear resistance and reduces subsurface plastic deformation of FeNiCrCoCu coatings under high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Increase the coating’s post-deposition annealing temperature from 700 °C (baseline) to 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding contact (≥700 °C) in an oxidizing environment at similar normal loads and sliding speeds for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Thickness and composition of the thermally grown oxide tribofilm on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: Elevated annealing temperature promotes oxide layer growth and stability. Under sliding at high temperature, this thicker tribofilm impedes metal–metal asperity contact, lowering friction and wear while mitigating subsurface dislocation activity and microcracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the 700 °C baseline, coatings annealed at 900 °C will exhibit a thicker, more uniform oxide film, reduced wear rates, lower friction coefficients, and less subsurface plastic deformation.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating annealed at 700 °C, tested under the same high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected only in oxidizing atmospheres and at temperatures high enough to develop a protective oxide tribofilm; exceedingly high temperatures or non-oxidizing environments may invalidate the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Other factors (e.g., nanostructural changes, secondary phase precipitation) may also affect surface hardness and tribofilm stability, and could overshadow or counteract the predicted oxide-driven improvements under certain conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one unannealed (control), one annealed at 700 °C, and one annealed at 900 °C. Subject all samples to identical high-temperature sliding tests in air, measuring friction coefficient, wear volume, cross-sectional oxide thickness, and near-surface microstructure.
measurements: Wear volume and wear track morphology
Friction coefficient over multiple sliding cycles
Cross-sectional TEM/SEM analysis of oxide layers
Microhardness in and near the wear track
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 900 °C-annealed coatings do not exhibit a demonstrably thicker or more stable oxide film accompanied by reduced wear and lower near-surface deformation relative to the 700 °C or unannealed coatings, the hypothesis is falsified.

This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa). Meanwhile, during HTXRD in air, corundum oxides formed initially at 550 °C, which is different from what ThermoCalc predicted. The formation of corundom (Mn2O3) during the experiment can be explained with the increase in temperature, and the initially formed corundom oxide changed to spinel (Mn3O4) at a higher temperature (950 °C). If considering oxides that form at a higher temperature such as 950, 1000, and 1050 °C, the ThermoCalc-predicted spinel oxide type is the same as the experimentally found spinel oxide. However, ThermoCalc predicts Co as a second major element in the spinel oxide that can form, but during the experiment, spinel oxides contain only Mn, Cr, and Fe (i.e., Mn3O4, MnCr2O4, and Fe3Mn3O8). cited_evidence.kind: web:6. Friction Coefficient and Wear Mechanism
cited_evidence.text: The presence of an oxide film on the surface that experiences wear significantly affects the performance of the coatings in terms of wear. An XPS study was performed to examine the composition and valence state of the oxide coating. The findings are presented in Figure 15. An ultrasonic amplitude of 5 μm leads to a significantly stronger O peak compared to the Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mn peaks. This indicates the existence of metallic oxides comprising these metal elements on the worn surface, which further reveals that the wear process at 5 µm is abrasive and oxidative due to the presence of a robust oxide coating on the worn surface.

decision.trend: Earlier tribological studies on high-entropy alloys point to microstructure–property relationships driving wear resistance, especially at elevated temperatures. First, CoCrFeMnNi-based coatings (PMC7311485) showed that friction and wear can be markedly influenced by near-surface dynamic structural refinement, sometimes leading to “inverse Hall-Petch” behavior. Next, investigations into refractory high-entropy alloys (PMC11206460) revealed that high-temperature mechanical strength and deformation responses are closely linked with dislocation activity and phase stability, highlighting the importance of understanding how thermal exposure modulates microstructure. More recently, FeCoNiMnCu coatings on steel substrates (PMC10908794) demonstrated that forming stable oxide layers at high temperature can promote better hardness and wear resistance, suggesting that interface and tribofilm evolution at elevated temperatures plays a decisive role in controlling friction and microscopic deformation in these systems.
decision.unsolved: Although it is clear that high-entropy alloy coatings can sustain good wear resistance and mechanical stability, the precise mechanism by which surface oxide layers and subsurface deformation structures interact at high temperatures remains poorly quantified. In particular, it is still unresolved whether oxide films, dynamic recrystallization, or secondary phase formation drives the enhanced wear resistance and micro-deformation behavior in FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings under high-temperature sliding.
decision.lever: Vary the post-deposition annealing temperature (e.g., 700 °C vs. 900 °C) to tune the thickness and composition of the oxide tribofilm formed at the coating surface.
decision.why: Recent observations (PMC10908794) suggest that stable oxide layers significantly improve wear performance and may alter near-surface dislocation behavior at high temperatures. By controlling the annealing temperature, one can regulate the oxidation kinetics and resultant tribofilm, thereby testing the hypothesis that these oxide scales dominate overall wear resistance and subsurface deformation in high-temperature sliding. If coatings annealed at higher temperature do not show improved wear behavior or modified subsurface deformation despite a thicker oxide layer, this result would falsify the proposed mechanism.
